questions.questionText: Let $\text{R(A, B, C, D, E)}$ be a relational schema with functional dependency set $\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\}$. Which of the following statements is correct? $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$. $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$. $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$. $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\text{R(A, B, C, D, E)}$ be a relational schema with functional dependency set $\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\}$.

Which of the following statements is correct?

  1. $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
  2. $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$.
  3. $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
  4. $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: A
options.text: $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: B
options.text: $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$.

options.label: C
options.text: $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: D
options.text: $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

questions.explanation: This is a basic fundamental question. To save time, we have  an important property: Any attribute that does NOT appear on the RHS of any functional dependency must be present in every candidate key. Given: \[ F = \{ A \to BC,\; CD \to E,\; E \to A \} \] RHS attributes = {B, C, E, A} Attribute \(D\) does NOT appear on the RHS. Hence, \(D\) must be present in every candidate key. Now eliminate options that do not contain \(D\). Remaining possibilities: \(AD, ED, CD\) Check closures: \[ (AD)^+ = ABCDE \] \[ (ED)^+ = ABCDE \] \[ (CD)^+ = ABCDE \] Thus, the only candidate keys are: \[ AD,\; ED,\; CD \] Correct option: \[ {(A)} \]

questions.questionText: In a relational database, a $\mathrm{B}+$ Tree Index is to be constructed for a relation on a key field. In a $\text{B+}$ Tree, a Node Pointer points to a sub-tree and a Data Record Pointer points to a block of database records. Let, Node size $=4096$ bytes, Node Pointer size $=10$ bytes, Search Key Field size $=11$ bytes and Data Record Pointer size $= 12$ bytes. The maximum number of Node Pointers that can be present in a non-leaf node of the $\text{B+}$ Tree is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.questionHtml:
In a relational database, a $\mathrm{B}+$ Tree Index is to be constructed for a relation on a key field. In a $\text{B+}$ Tree, a Node Pointer points to a sub-tree and a Data Record Pointer points to a block of database records.

Let, Node size $=4096$ bytes, Node Pointer size $=10$ bytes, Search Key Field size $=11$ bytes and Data Record Pointer size $= 12$ bytes.

The maximum number of Node Pointers that can be present in a non-leaf node of the $\text{B+}$ Tree is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Given: Block size = 4096 bytes   Node pointer size = 10 bytes   Search key size = 11 bytes   For a non-leaf node: If there are p node pointers, then there are (p - 1) search keys. Total size condition: \[ 10p + 11(p - 1) \le \lfloor 4096 \rfloor \] Expand: \[ 10p + 11p - 11 \le 4096 \] \[ 21p - 11 \le 4096 \] \[ 21p \le 4107 \] \[ p \le \frac{4107}{21} \] \[ p \le 195.57 \] Taking floor: \[ p = \left\lfloor \frac{4107}{21} \right\rfloor = 195 \] Final Answer: \[ \boxed{195} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a B+ Tree where the maximum number of key values in each leaf node is $2$ and the maximum number of pointers in each non-leaf node is $3$. Let the content of the B+ Tree be as shown in the figure.

Which of the following options denotes the key value(s) stored in the root node after inserting a key value $3$ in the given B+ Tree?

  1. $5$
  2. $8$
  3. $3$ and $5$
  4. $3, 5$ and $8$
questions.explanation: Note: In this question, we are not required to draw Full B+ tree to save time. Maximum keys in each leaf node = 2 Maximum pointers in each internal node = 3 Maximum keys in each internal node = 2 In a B+tree , we know that insertion always happens at root node.   Root: \[ [5 , 8] \] Leaf Nodes: \[ [1,5] \rightarrow [7,8] \rightarrow [9,12] \] Insert key = 3 Since $3 < 5$, it is inserted in the first leaf node: \[ [1,5] \Rightarrow [1,3,5] \] But a leaf can contain at most 2 keys.   Hence, overflow occurs and the node must be split. Split the leaf node: \[ [1,3,5] \Rightarrow [1,3] \quad \text{and} \quad [5] \]   Root becomes: \[ [3,5,8] \] Now the root has 3 keys, but it can hold at most 2 keys.   Hence, root overflow occurs. Split the root: \[ [3,5,8] \] Middle key $5$ moves up and becomes the new root. Final Root \[ \boxed{5} \] Correct Option: (A)

questions.questionText: Consider a table Employee(EmpID, TeamID), where the column EmpID (ID of an employee) is the primary key. The column TeamID denotes the team ID of the team of which the employee is a member. TeamID is a NOT NULL column. We want to display the size of the team (denoted as TeamSize) in which each employee is a member by using SQL. As an example, the desired output for the given Employee table is also shown in tabular form. Which of the following is/are correct? \[ \textbf{Employee} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamID} \\ \hline 1 & 8 \\ \hline 2 & 8 \\ \hline 3 & 8 \\ \hline 4 & 7 \\ \hline 5 & 7 \\ \hline 6 & 9 \\ \hline \end{array} \] \[ \textbf{Output} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamSize} \\ \hline 1 & 3 \\ \hline 2 & 3 \\ \hline 3 & 3 \\ \hline 4 & 2 \\ \hline 5 & 2 \\ \hline 6 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array} \] SELECT E.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM Employee AS E, (SELECT TeamID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B WHERE E.TeamID = B.TeamID SELECT A.EmpID, COUNT(B.TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, Employee AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID AND A.EmpID = B.EmpID GROUP BY A.EmpID SELECT B.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM (SELECT EmpID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY EmpID) AS B SELECT A.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, (SELECT COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID

Consider a table Employee(EmpID, TeamID), where the column EmpID (ID of an employee) is the primary key. The column TeamID denotes the team ID of the team of which the employee is a member. TeamID is a NOT NULL column.

We want to display the size of the team (denoted as TeamSize) in which each employee is a member by using SQL. As an example, the desired output for the given Employee table is also shown in tabular form.

Which of the following is/are correct?

\[
\textbf{Employee}
\]

\[

\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{EmpID} & \text{TeamID} \\
\hline
1 & 8 \\
\hline
2 & 8 \\
\hline
3 & 8 \\
\hline
4 & 7 \\
\hline
5 & 7 \\
\hline
6 & 9 \\

\[
\textbf{Output}
\]

\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{EmpID} & \text{TeamSize} \\
\hline
1 & 3 \\
\hline
2 & 3 \\
\hline
3 & 3 \\
\hline
4 & 2 \\
\hline

\hline
6 & 1 \\
\hline

\]

  1. SELECT E.EmpID, B.TeamSize
FROM Employee AS E, (SELECT TeamID, COUNT(TeamID) AS
TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B
WHERE E.TeamID = B.TeamID
  2. SELECT A.EmpID, COUNT(B.TeamID) AS TeamSize
FROM Employee AS A, Employee AS B
WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID AND A.EmpID = B.EmpID
GROUP BY A.EmpID

  3. SELECT B.EmpID, B.TeamSize
FROM (SELECT EmpID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize
FROM Employee GROUP BY EmpID) AS B

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT A.EmpID, COUNT(B.TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, Employee AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID AND A.EmpID = B.EmpID GROUP BY A.EmpID

options.label: C
options.text: SELECT B.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM (SELECT EmpID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY EmpID) AS B

options.label: D
options.text: SELECT A.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, (SELECT COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID

questions.explanation: In this question, we need to focus on the attributes used in the GROUP BY clause. Since we are asked to find the team size, the grouping must be done based on TeamID , not EmpID . Options B and C are clearly incorrect because they group by EmpID , whereas the requirement is to group rows based on TeamID . Team size is obtained by grouping on TeamID and applying COUNT(column_name) to get the number of employees in each team. When it comes to option D, the issue is that there is no TeamID present in the inner query result. Because of this, it is not possible to match with the condition A.TeamID = B.TeamID after the cross product, making the query invalid. Finally, option A works correctly because the inner query provides the necessary TeamID , which allows proper matching after the cross product and results in the correct team size for each employee.

Let $A_{22}$ be a multi-valued attribute. $A_{11}$ and $A_{21}$ are the primary keys of $\text{E1}$ and $\text{E2}$, respectively.

Let $\text{R12}$ be a many-to-many relationship between $\text{E1}$ and $\text{E2}$. Participation of both $\text{E1}$ and $\text{E2}$ in $\text{R12}$ is total.

questions.explanation: Given: Entity E1(A11, A12, A13) Primary key: A11   Entity E2(A21, A22, A23)   Primary key: A21   A22 is a multi-valued attribute. R12 is a many-to-many relationship between E1 and E2. Participation of both E1 and E2 in R12 is total. Step 1: Convert Entity E1 \[ E1(A11, A12, A13) \] This gives 1 relation. Step 2: Convert Entity E2 Since A22 is multi-valued, it must be represented separately. Main relation: \[ E21(A21, A23) \] Multi-valued attribute relation: \[ E22(A21, A22) \] Primary key of this relation is (A21, A22). So far, we have 3 relations. Step 3: Convert Many-to-Many Relationship R12 A many-to-many relationship requires a separate relation: \[ R12(A11, A21) \] Primary key: (A11, A21) Total participation only enforces participation constraints and does not eliminate the need for this relation. Step 4: Count Total Relations \[ E1,\; E21,\; E22,\; R12 \] Total number of relations: \[ \boxed{4} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 24 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya

questions.questionHtml:
Consider concurrent execution of two transactions $T 1$ and $T 2$ in a DBMS, both of which access a data object $A$. For these two transactions to not conflict on $A$, which one of the following statements must be true?

  1. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ only read $A$
  2. $T 1$ reads $A$ and $T 2$ writes $A$
  3. $T 1$ writes $A$ and $T 2$ reads $A$
  4. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ write $A$
questions.explanation: Answer: Option A In a DBMS, two operations on the same data object Q are said to be in conflict if at least one of them is a Write operation. Conflict Conditions For two transactions T1 and T2 accessing the same data object Q are said to be in conflict if at least one of them is a Write operation. Read-Read (R-R): No Conflict. Both transactions are only viewing the data; the state of $Q$ remains unchanged. Read-Write (R-W): Conflict. One transaction reads while the other updates, leading to potential inconsistency. Write-Read (W-R): Conflict. Known as a "Dirty Read" if the write hasn't been committed. Write-Write (W-W): Conflict. Known as a "Blind Write" or "Lost Update" problem. Therefore, for T1 and T2 to not conflict , the only valid scenario is when both T1 and T2 only read Q. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/concurrency-control-in-dbms/  akash_kumar 9 answered Feb 25 akash_kumar 9 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Although I

questions.questionText: In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $\text{F}$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $\text{F}$ is called the closure of $\text{F}$. To compute the closure of $\text{F}$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X, Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows. Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$ Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $X Z \rightarrow Y Z$ for any Z Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$ The additional rule of Union is defined as follows. Union: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Y Z$ It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof? Reflexivity, Augmentation, and Transitivity Reflexivity and Augmentation Transitivity Augmentation and Transitivity
questions.questionHtml:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $\text{F}$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $\text{F}$ is called the closure of $\text{F}$. To compute the closure of $\text{F}$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X, Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$

Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $X Z \rightarrow Y Z$ for any Z

Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Y Z$

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?

  1. Reflexivity, Augmentation, and Transitivity
  2. Reflexivity and Augmentation
  3. Transitivity
  4. Augmentation and Transitivity
questions.explanation: Answer : D We know $X \to Y$. $X \to Y$ with $X$ itself. Found: $XX \to XY$, simplify to $X \to XY$ . We know $X \to Z$. $X \to Z$ with $Y$. Result: $XY \to YZ$ . Since we have $X \to XY$ and $XY \to YZ$. UNION: $X \to YZ$ . Srinivas_Chundi answered Mar 3 Srinivas_Chundi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true
questions.questionHtml:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.


$\text{S1}$: A hash index must be a dense index
$\text{S1}$: A $B^{+}$ tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?

  1. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true
  2. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false
  3. $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false
  4. $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true
questions.explanation: S1: A hash index must be a dense index Status: True Reason: Every unique search-key value requires a corresponding entry in the hash table to be located by the hash function. By definition, an index that tracks every search-key value is a dense index . S2: A B+ tree index can be a sparse index Status: True Reason: While B+ trees are often dense, they can be sparse when acting as a primary (clustering) index. In this mode, they only store entries for a subset of keys (usually one per data block), which helps minimize index size. so option A is correct

questions.questionText: Consider a relational database schema with two relations $R(P, Q)$ and $S(X, Y)$. Let $E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}$ be a tuple relational calculus expression. Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to $E$ ? $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . X} S\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . X=R . Q} R\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . Y} S\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . Y=R . Q} R\right)$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations $R(P, Q)$ and $S(X, Y)$.

Let $E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}$ be a tuple relational calculus expression.

Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to $E$ ?

  1. $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . X} S\right)$
  2. $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . X=R . Q} R\right)$
  3. $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . Y} S\right)$
  4. $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . Y=R . Q} R\right)$
questions.explanation: The expression \( E \) describes a set of tuples \(\langle u \rangle\) such that there exists a tuple \(\langle u, v \rangle\) in relation \( R \) and a tuple \(\langle v, w \rangle\) in relation \( S \). This implies that \( v \) is a common attribute between the two relations, specifically \( R.Q \) and \( S.X \). Now, let's translate this into relational algebra: 1. Join Condition: We need to perform a join between \( R \) and \( S \) on the condition \( R.Q = S.X \) because \( v \) is the common attribute. 2. Projection: After joining, we are interested in the attribute \( P \) from relation \( R \). Therefore, the equivalent relational algebra expression is: \[ \Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R.Q = S.X} S\right) \] This expression selects the attribute \( P \) from relation \( R \), where \( R.Q = S.X \) in the joined tables, which aligns with the tuple relational calculus expression given in the problem. questions.questionText: Consider the relation $R(A,B,C,D,E)$ with the following functional dependencies: \[ A \rightarrow BC,\qquad CD \rightarrow E,\qquad E \rightarrow A. \] What are the candidate keys of $R$ ? $\{AD,\; CD,\; ED\}$ $\{AC,\; CD,\; DE\}$ $\{AD,\; CE,\; CD\}$ $\{A,\; CD,\; ED\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the relation $R(A,B,C,D,E)$ with the following functional dependencies:
\[
A \rightarrow BC,\qquad CD \rightarrow E,\qquad E \rightarrow A.
\]
What are the candidate keys of $R$ ?

  1. $\{AD,\; CD,\; ED\}$

  2. $\{AC,\; CD,\; DE\}$

  3. $\{AD,\; CE,\; CD\}$

  4. $\{A,\; CD,\; ED\}$
questions.explanation: Answer: (A) {AD, CD, ED} To find the candidate keys, we determine the closure of each potential key attribute set. A set of attributes $X$ is a candidate key if its closure, $X^+$, includes all attributes in $R(A, B, C, D, E)$. The given functional dependencies (FDs) are $A \to BC$, $CD \to E$, and $E \to A$. Note that the image likely has a typo and the third FD should be $E \to A$. Check A: $AD^+ = \{A, D\}$ (start with A and D) $A \to BC$, so add B and C: $\{A, B, C, D\}$ $CD \to E$, so add E: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $AD$ is a candidate key. Check CD: $CD^+ = \{C, D\}$ (start with C and D) $CD \to E$, so add E: $\{C, D, E\}$ $E \to A$, so add A: $\{A, C, D, E\}$ $A \to BC$, so add B: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $CD$ is a candidate key. Check ED: $ED^+ = \{E, D\}$ (start with E and D) $E \to A$, so add A: $\{A, D, E\}$ $A \to BC$, so add B and C: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $ED$ is a candidate key. All three attribute sets in option A are candidate keys. The other options contain sets that are not keys

questions.questionHtml:
Consider two relations: $$R(A, B), \quad \quad S(E, C)$$Attribute $A$ is the primary key of relation $R$.  

Attribute $E$ in relation $S$ is a foreign key that references $A$ in $R$.

Which of the following operations will NEVER violate the foreign key constraint?

  1. Delete a record from $R$
     
  2. Delete a record from $S$
     
  3. Insert a record into $R$
     
  4. Insert a record into $S$
questions.explanation: Answer: (B) Delete a record from S & (C) Insert a record into R Explanation (A) Delete a record from R: This operation can violate the foreign key constraint if the record being deleted from table R has its primary key value referenced by one or more records in table S. (B) Delete a record from S: Deleting a record from the referencing table S does not violate the constraint because it removes a reference to a primary key value in R. The referenced value in R still exists. (C) Insert a record into R: Inserting a new record into the referenced table R does not violate the constraint because it introduces a new primary key value that can be referenced by records in S in the future. (D) Insert a record into S: This operation can violate the foreign key constraint if the value inserted into attribute E (the foreign key) does not already exist as a primary key value in attribute A of table R. questions.questionText: In the question, the following three of Armstrong's axioms are given: Reflexivity (Trivial), Augmentation, and Transitivity. Now, we want to prove that $$ \{X \rightarrow Y,\; X \rightarrow Z\} \Rightarrow X \rightarrow YZ $$ using only the above three Armstrong's axioms. Use the minimum number of axioms from the given three to prove the result. Which of the following options can prove the result? Reflexivity, Transitivity Reflexivity, Augmentation Transitivity, Augmentation Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity
questions.questionHtml:
In the question, the following three of Armstrong's axioms are given:
Reflexivity (Trivial), Augmentation, and Transitivity.

Now, we want to prove that
$$
\{X \rightarrow Y,\; X \rightarrow Z\} \Rightarrow X \rightarrow YZ
$$
using only the above three Armstrong's axioms.

Use the minimum number of axioms from the given three to prove the result.
Which of the following options can prove the result?

  1. Reflexivity, Transitivity
     
  2. Reflexivity, Augmentation
     
  3. Transitivity, Augmentation
     
  4. Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity
questions.explanation: The Problem We need to prove the Union Rule : $$\{ X \rightarrow Y, X \rightarrow Z \} \Rightarrow X \rightarrow YZ$$ Using the minimum number of Armstrong's Axioms from this list: Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$. Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $XZ \rightarrow YZ$. Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$. Step-by-Step Solution To prove $X \rightarrow YZ$ from the given $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$: Apply Augmentation: Take the given $X \rightarrow Y$. Augment both sides with $X$. Result: $XX \rightarrow XY$, which simplifies to $X \rightarrow XY$ . Apply Augmentation again: Take the given $X \rightarrow Z$. Augment both sides with $Y$. Result: $XY \rightarrow YZ$ . Apply Transitivity: Now we have $X \rightarrow XY$ (from step 1) and $XY \rightarrow YZ$ (from step 2). By transitivity: $X \rightarrow YZ$ . Axioms used: Augmentation, Transitivity. Correct Option: 3. Transitivity, Augmentation

questions.questionText: In indexing, we have two types of index: Dense Index and Sparse Index . In a dense index, we store an index entry for every record, while in a sparse index we do not store an index entry for every record. Which of the following is true regarding the given two statements? $\mathrm{S1}:$ Hash index MUST have dense indexing. $\mathrm{S2}:$ B+ tree can have sparse index. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are true $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are false $\mathrm{S1}$ is true, $\mathrm{S2}$ is false $\mathrm{S1}$ is false, $\mathrm{S2}$ is true
questions.questionHtml:
In indexing, we have two types of index: Dense Index and Sparse Index.
In a dense index, we store an index entry for every record, while in a sparse index we do not store an index entry for every record. Which of the following is true regarding the given two statements?

$\mathrm{S1}:$ Hash index MUST have dense indexing.

$\mathrm{S2}:$ B+ tree can have sparse index.
 

  1. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are true
     
  2. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are false
     
  3. $\mathrm{S1}$ is true, $\mathrm{S2}$ is false
     
  4. $\mathrm{S1}$ is false, $\mathrm{S2}$ is true
questions.explanation: Option A: S1, S2 both are true Statement 1: Hash index MUST have dense indexing. This statement is generally considered  true  in the context of database indexing fundamentals. A hash index uses a hash function to directly map a search key to a specific "bucket" (which might be a disk block). For efficient retrieval, every search key value generally needs to have an entry in the hash structure to ensure the correct bucket can be found quickly. The hash index typically stores all search keys and their pointers, fitting the definition of a dense index. If it were sparse, the collision handling and search efficiency would be severely degraded, effectively requiring a linear scan within large buckets which defeats the purpose of hashing for speed. Statement 2: B+ tree can have sparse index. This statement is  true . B+ trees are commonly used for multi-level indexing. The non-leaf (internal) nodes in a B+ tree inherently form a hierarchy of sparse indexes on the leaf nodes.

questions.explanation: Given Disk size = 2^34 bytes Block size = 2^11 bytes Total number of blocks 2^34 / 2^11 = 2^23 So total blocks = 2^23 . Size required to store all block addresses Each block address = 32 bits = 4 bytes = 2^2 bytes So total size needed to store all addresses: 2^23 x 2^2 = 2^25 bytes Number of blocks required to store this overhead 2^25 / 2^11 = 2^14 >> So 2^14 = 16384 is the answer Damin_Risho answered Feb 12 • edited Feb 17 by Damin_Risho Damin_Risho comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Question 9

Let R(A) be a relation that contains both integer and NULL values in attribute A.

Consider the following two queries:

Query 1:

SELECT * FROM R WHERE A NOT IN (5, 10, NULL);

Query 2:

SELECT * FROM R WHERE A <> 5 AND A <> 10 AND A IS NOT NULL;

Which of the following statements is/are false?

A. Query 1 and Query 2 return same tuples.
B. Query 1 will not return any tuple for any value of A.
C. Query 1 returns rows where A is not NULL and is neither 5 nor 10.
D. Query 2 will return all rows where A is neither 5 nor 10.

options.label: A
options.text: Query 1 and Query 2 return same tuples.

options.label: B
options.text: Query 1 will not return any tuple for any value of

options.label: C
options.text: Query 1 returns rows where A is not NULL and is neither 5 nor 10.

options.label: D
options.text: Query 2 will return all rows where A is neither 5 nor 10.

questions.explanation: Answer - A, C The expression  A NOT IN (5, 10, NULL) is equivalent to (A <> 5) AND (A <> 10) AND (A <> NULL). Query 1: But A <> NULL always yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Because the overall condition uses AND, the entire predicate becomes UNKNOWN for every row. UNKNOWN acts as FALSE in the WHERE clause. Therefore, Query 1 returns no rows at all (for any value of A). Query 2: A <> 5 AND A <> 10 AND A IS NOT NULL → This correctly returns rows where A is neither 5 nor 10 and also not NULL.

questions.questionText: A database of research articles in a journal uses the following schema: (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, YEAR, PRICE) The primary key is (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) and the following functional dependencies exist in the schema. (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) → TITLE (VOLUME, NUMBER) → YEAR (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) → PRICE The database is redesigned to use the following schemas: (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, PRICE) (VOLUME, NUMBER, YEAR) Which is the weakest normal form that the new database satisfies, but the old one does not? (a) 1NF (b) 2NF (c) 3NF (d) BCNF
questions.questionHtml:
A database of research articles in a journal uses the following schema:
(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, YEAR, PRICE)
The primary key is (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) and the following functional dependencies exist in the schema.

(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) → TITLE

(VOLUME, NUMBER) → YEAR

(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE) → PRICE

The database is redesigned to use the following schemas:
(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, PRICE)
(VOLUME, NUMBER, YEAR)

Which is the weakest normal form that the new database satisfies, but the old one does not?
(a) 1NF (b) 2NF
(c) 3NF (d) BCNF
questions.explanation: Primary key is {VOLUME, NUMBER,STARTPAGE,ENDPAGE} Second fd is proper subset of primary key determining a non prime attribute which violation of 2nf. Hence the schema belongs to 1NF. The database is redesigned schemas: Table1 :(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, PRICE)       Preserved 1,3 FD's and No proper subset of candidate key determining non prime attribute . Hence 2NF        From 1,3 FD's preserved on table 1, every FD superkey determinging non prime attribute. Hence 3NF Table2 :(VOLUME, NUMBER, YEAR)        Preserved 2nd FD. No proper subset of candidate key determining no primeattribute. Hence 2NF.        From 2nd FD, the FD candidate key determining a non prime attribute. Hence 3NF. Hence ultimate new schema in 3NF. questions.questionText: ​​​​​If a relational decomposition is not dependency-preserving, which one of the following relational operators will be executed more frequently in order to maintain the dependencies? Selection Projection Join Set union
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​If a relational decomposition is not dependency-preserving, which one of the following relational operators will be executed more frequently in order to maintain the dependencies?

  1. Selection
  2. Projection
  3. Join
  4. Set union
questions.explanation: Selection (\(\sigma\)): Selection is used to retrieve a subset of rows (tuples) from a relation based on a condition. Projection (\(\pi\)): Projection is used to retrieve specific columns (attributes) from a relation. Set Union (\(\cup\)): Set Union is used to combine tuples from two relations that have the same schema . However, dependency loss occurs across different relations. Join (\(\bowtie\)): Join combines decomposed relations together based on common attributes. If a dependency is lost due to decomposition, Join helps reconstruct the original relation. questions.questionText: ​​​​An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account $A$ attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. $10000$ each from account $A$ to account $B$. Both transactions read the same value, Rs.$11000$, as the initial balance in $A$ and were allowed to go through. $B$ was credited Rs.$10000$ twice. $A$ was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. $1000$. Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system? Atomicity Consistency Isolation Durability
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account $A$ attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. $10000$ each from account $A$ to account $B$. Both transactions read the same value, Rs.$11000$, as the initial balance in $A$ and were allowed to go through. $B$ was credited Rs.$10000$ twice. $A$ was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. $1000$.

Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?

  1. Atomicity
  2. Consistency
  3. Isolation
  4. Durability
questions.explanation: Given: Account $A$ has $\text{Rs. 11,000.}$ Two simultaneous transfers of $\text{Rs. 10,000}$ each are attempted. Account $B$ is credited twice (total $\text{Rs. 20,000}$). Account $A$ is debited only once (final balance $\text{Rs. 1,000}$). Analysis of ACID Properties: Atomicity: Ensures all parts of a transaction are completed or none are. Each transfer individually was complete (money was debited from $A$ and credited to $B$), so atomicity is likely not violated. $✘$  Not necessarily violated. Consistency: Ensures that the database moves from one valid state to another. If $\text{Rs. 20,000}$ was credited to $B$, $\text{Rs. 20,000}$ should be debited from $A$. But only $\text{Rs. 10,000}$ was debited. This breaks balance rules. $✓$ Violated. Isolation: Ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. Both transactions read the same initial balance ( $\text{Rs. 11,000}$) and proceeded independently, leading to an incorrect final state. This is a classic lost up

questions.questionHtml:
​​​​Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.
\[
\begin{array}{l}
R 1(A, B, C, D, E):\{D \rightarrow E, E A \rightarrow B, E B \rightarrow C\} \\
R 2(A, B, C, D):\{A \rightarrow D, A \rightarrow B, C \rightarrow A\}
\end{array}
\]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

  1. $R 1$ is in $3$ NF
  2. $R 2$ is in $3$ NF
  3. $R 1$ is NOT in $3$ NF
  4. $R 2$ is NOT in $3$ NF
questions.explanation: A relation is in 3NF if for every functional dependency \( X \to Y \), if \( X \) is a superkey, or \( Y \) is a prime attribute. \( R_1(A, B, C, D, E) \) \begin{align*} D &\to E \\ EA &\to B \\ EB &\to C \end{align*} \[AD^+ = \{ A, B, C, D, E \}\] \( AD \) is a candidate key. \( D \to E \) (Violation: \( D \) is not a superkey, \( E \) is not prime). \( EA \to B \) (Violation: \( EA \) is not a superkey, \( B \) is not prime). \( EB \to C \) (Violation: \( EB \) is not a superkey, \( C \) is not prime). \( R_1 \) is not in 3NF. \( R_2(A, B, C, D) \)} \begin{align*} A &\to D \\ A &\to B \\ C &\to A \end{align*} \[C^+ = \{ A, B, C, D \}\] \( C \) is a candidate key. \( A \to D \) (Violation: \( A \) is not a superkey, \( D \) is not prime). \( A \to B \) (Violation: \( A \) is not a superkey, \( B \) is not prime). \( C \to A \) (No violation: \( C \) is a superkey). \( R_2 \) is not in 3NF. questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​Which of the following file organizations is/are $\text{I/O}$ efficient for the scan operation in $\text{DBMS}$?

  1. Sorted
  2. Heap
  3. Unclustered tree index
  4. Unclustered hash index
questions.explanation: A  sorted  file organization ensures that records are stored in a sequential order, which is optimal for scan operations since the data can be accessed sequentially with minimal I/O overhead. In a  heap  file organization, records are stored without any specific order. Although not as efficient as sorted files, a heap file still allows sequential scans across all records with moderate I/O efficiency. Options C (Unclustered tree index) and D (Unclustered hash index) are not I/O efficient for scans because they involve random access to data blocks, leading to higher I/O costs. Hence, the correct answer is A and B. If you liked this answer, please consider upvoting it.

codeBlocks:
No, composite and multivalued attributes are two different concepts.

Composite Attribute:
This type of attribute can be broken down into smaller components.
Example: Address can be split into Street, City, State, and Pincode.

Multivalued Attribute:
This attribute can store more than one value for the same entity.
Example: A single person having multiple addresses such as:
Bengaluru – 560001, Karnataka
Dwarka, New Delhi – 110078
Pune – 411027, Maharashtra
Also, in (1NF), a table should not contain composite attributes or multivalued attributes — all values must be atomic (indivisible).

options.label: D
options.text: $\mathbf{R}$ cannot have more than one candidate key

questions.questionText: Consider a database of fixed-length records, stored as an ordered file. The database has $25,000$ records, with each record being $100$ bytes, of which the primary key occupies $15$ bytes. The data file is block-aligned in that each data record is fully contained within a block. The database is indexed by a primary index file, which is also stored as a block-aligned ordered file. The figure below depicts this indexing scheme. Suppose the block size of the file system is $1024$ bytes, and a pointer to a block occupies $5$ bytes. The system uses binary search on the index file to search for a record with a given key. You may assume that a binary search on an index file of $b$ blocks takes $\left\lceil\log _{2} b\right\rceil$ block accesses in the worst case. Given a key, the number of block accesses required to identify the block in the data file that may contain a record with the key, in the worst case, is _____________.

Consider the relational database with the following four schemas and their respective instances.

  • Student(sNo, sName, dNo) Dept(dNo, dName)
  • Course(cNo, cName, dNo) Register(sNo, cNo)

$$\begin{array} {|c|c|c|} \hline  & \text{Students} & \\ \hline  \text{sNo}  & \text{sName} &  \text{dNo} \\ \hline \text{S01} & \text{James} & \text{D01} \\ \hline \text{S02} & \text{Rocky} & \text{D01} \\ \hline \text{S03} & \text{Jackson} & \text{D02} \\ \hline \text{S04} & \text{Jane} & \text{D01} \\ \hline \text{S05} & \text{Milli} & \text{D02}\\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array} {|c|c|} \hline  & \text{Depth} \\ \hline  \text{dNo}  & \text{dName} \\ \hline \text{D01} & \text{CSE} \\ \hline \text{D02} & \text{EEE} \\ \hline  \end{array} \quad \begin{array} {|c|c|c|} \hline  & \text{Course} & \\ \hline  \text{cNo}  & \text{cName} &  \text{dNo} \\ \hline \text{C11} & \text{DS} & \text{D01} \\ \hline \text{C12} & \text{OS} & \text{D01} \\ \hline \text{C21} & \text{DE} & \text{D02} \\ \hline \text{C22} & \text{PT} & \text{D02} \\ \hline \text{C23} & \text{CV} & \text{D03}\\ \hline \end{array}\quad \begin{array} {|c|c|} \hline  & \text{Register} \\ \hline  \text{sNo}  & \text{cNo} \\ \hline \text{S01} & \text{C11} \\ \hline \text{S01} & \text{C12} \\ \hline \text{S02} & \text{C11} \\ \hline  \text{S03} & \text{C21}\\ \hline \text{S03} & \text{C22} \\ \hline \text{S03} & \text{C23} \\ \hline \text{S04} & \text{C11} \\ \hline \text{S04} & \text{C12} \\ \hline \text{S05} & \text{C11}\\ \hline \text{S05} & \text{C21} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$\textbf{SQL query}$

SELECT * FROM Student AS S WHERE NOT EXIST

  (SELECT cNo FROM Course WHERE dNo = “D01”

         EXCEPT

    SELECT cNo FROM Register WHERE sNo = S.sNo)

The number of rows returned by the above $\text{SQL}$ query is ____________.

$$\overset{\text{Catalogue}} {\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \underline{\text{sno}} & \underline{\text{pno}} & \text{cost} \\ \hline S1 & P1 & 150 \\ \hline S1 & P2 & 50 \\ \hline S1 & P3 & 100 \\ \hline S2 & P4 & 200 \\ \hline S2 & P5 & 250 \\ \hline S3 & P1 & 250 \\ \hline S3 & P2 & 150 \\ \hline S3 & P5 & 300 \\ \hline S3 & P4 & 250 \\ \hline \end{array}} \quad \overset{ \text{Suppliers} }{\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \underline{\text{sno}} & \text{sname} & \text{location} \\ \hline S1 & \text{M/s Royal furniture} & \text{Delhi}\\ \hline S2 & \text{M/s Balaji furniture} & \text{Bangalore} \\ \hline S3 & \text{M/s Premium furniture} & \text{Chennai} \\ \hline \end{array}} \quad \overset{\text{Parts}}{\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \underline{\text{pno}} & \text{pname} & \text{part_spec} \\ \hline P1 & \text{Table} & \text{Wood} \\ \hline P2 & \text{Chair} & \text{Wood} \\ \hline P3 & \text{Table} & \text{Steel} \\ \hline P4 & \text{Almirah} & \text{Steel} \\ \hline P5 & \text{Almirah} & \text{Wood} \\ \hline  \end{array}}$$

The primary key of each table is indicated by underlining the constituent fields.

SELECT s.sno, s.sname
FROM Suppliers s, Catalogue c
WHERE s.sno=c.sno AND
    cost > (SELECT AVG (cost)
            FROM Catalogue
            WHERE pno = ‘P4’
            GROUP BY pno) ;

The number of rows returned by the above SQL query is

  1. $4$
  2. $5$
  3. $0$
  4. $2$
